draft_text:
# The Boutique That Sells What Cannot Be Sold

Imagine walking into a shop where the mannequins wear survival gear designed not for Arctic expeditions or Silicon Valley doomsday preppers, but for mothers searching the Mexican desert for the bones of their children. The price tags list not euros but years of grief, hectares of scrubland combed on hands and knees, bodies counted and uncounted. This is the conceit at the heart of Backyard [A Field to Search], and it is precisely the kind of fiction that makes certain truths speakable.

On 23 April, Studio Я at the Maxim Gorki Theater hosts the lecture-performance iteration of this project by Laura Uribe and Sabina Aldana, two artists working under the umbrella of L.A.S. [Laboratory of Sustainable Artists]. Since 2018, they have been investigating enforced disappearances in Mexico — a crisis whose scale defies comprehension. [~When Uribe and Aldana began their research, the official count of disappeared persons stood at roughly 32,000; it now exceeds 130,000.|This trajectory is documented in the Gorki's own programme notes and aligns with widely reported Mexican government figures, though the true number is almost certainly higher.~] The arithmetic alone is staggering: a fourfold increase in seven years, a rate that renders each individual case statistically invisible even as the human weight of each one remains absolute.

The format they have chosen — a speculative pop-up boutique — is both absurd and lethally precise. Backyard presents itself as a retail space selling "multifunctional designer clothing for survival in the Global South," along with tools for searching for bodies and, in a detail that cuts like glass, women's underwear "against disappearance." The retail framework is a Trojan horse. Consumerism is the language much of the world speaks most fluently, and Uribe and Aldana weaponise it, forcing the audience into the discomfort of browsing products whose existence indicts the conditions that necessitate them. There is a lineage here that runs through the work of artists like Santiago Sierra, Thomas Hirschhorn, and the tactical media collectives of the 1990s — art that appropriates commercial or bureaucratic structures not to celebrate them but to make their violence legible. But Backyard is distinguished by something those precedents often lacked: the artists have spent years physically embedded in the search. They have joined self-organised search brigades — citizens, mostly women, mostly relatives of the disappeared — trekking through mountains, desert sand, and scrubland, looking for what the state will not look for.

This is the tension the lecture-performance navigates. On one hand, fiction as provocation: the theatre becomes a shop, the shop becomes an archive, the archive becomes a space where what "cannot be exhibited" is exhibited and what "must not be sold" is sold. On the other, a firsthand account of seven years moving through landscapes of state-sanctioned erasure. [~Coverage of L.A.S. outside of German-language theatre programming is sparse — a handful of references in the Gorki's own materials and event listings, but little independent critical writing in English.|I am working primarily from the theatre's programme notes and one detailed German-language description.~] What I can trace suggests that the project first materialised at the Gorki earlier in 2025 as a performative installation in the theatre's KIOSK space — a hybrid of pop-up store, workshop, and archive. This lecture iteration revisits and updates that earlier work, distilling its spatial sprawl into the more concentrated format of spoken address and demonstration.

Studio Я is a fitting container. The Gorki's experimental wing has, under the artistic directorship of Şermin Langhoff since 2013, become one of Berlin's most committed spaces for what the theatre calls post-migrant narratives — work that takes seriously the perspectives of those whose stories European institutions have historically told about rather than with. The building itself carries its own palimpsest of forced transformations: built in 1827 as a concert hall for the Sing-Akademie zu Berlin, confiscated by Soviet occupying forces after the Second World War, renamed after Maxim Gorky in 1952 as a "socialist model theatre," and reinvented once more after reunification. A building that has been claimed, repurposed, and re-narrated by successive powers is not a neutral backdrop for a project about people whom the state has made to vanish.

The lecture sits within the 7th Berliner Herbstsalon, the Gorki's recurring festival programme titled ЯE:IMAGINE: THE RED HOUSE. The performer Yanina Cerón joins Uribe and Aldana on stage. The piece is delivered in Spanish with English surtitles — a choice that keeps the work anchored in its linguistic origin rather than smoothing it into the frictionless English of international art speak. Expect something between a TED talk and its own demolition: the trappings of the lecture format (slides, perhaps objects from the boutique's inventory, the cadences of explanation and address) deployed against themselves, interrupted by testimony, by image, by the sheer accumulation of numbers that refuse to stay abstract.

What Backyard does with the format of retail is not unlike what forensic architecture does with the format of the courtroom exhibit, or what Milo Rau does with the format of the tribunal — it borrows a structure whose authority people already accept, then fills it with content that structure was never designed to hold. The difference is that Uribe and Aldana's borrowed structure is not the law or journalism but commerce. And commerce, unlike the law, does not pretend to care about justice. It pretends to care about you — the consumer, the individual with desires. So when the boutique offers you a garment designed to help a body survive, or to help a body be found, it asks: what kind of market is this? Who is the customer? Who set the conditions under which such products become necessary?

[~The figure of 130,000 disappeared in Mexico makes it one of the largest crises of enforced disappearance globally, comparable in scale to the desaparecidos of Argentina's Dirty War multiplied many times over.|The Argentine figure is commonly cited at 30,000; Mexico's crisis has received less consolidated international attention despite its greater numerical scale. Multiple human rights organisations corroborate the order of magnitude.~]

There is something important about this work appearing in Berlin rather than Mexico City. Not because European audiences need to be educated — that framing is patronising to everyone involved — but because the global supply chains of violence are not contained by borders, and the mechanisms of disappearance (corruption, narco-state entanglement, institutional indifference) are enabled by international economic structures in which European nations are participants, not bystanders. The boutique metaphor sharpens this: if you can buy the survival gear, you are already implicated in the economy that makes it necessary.

I cannot tell you what it feels like to sit in Studio Я and hear Uribe describe walking through scrubland with a dead person's mother. I can tell you that the architecture of this project — the collision of retail fantasy and forensic reality, the use of fiction not as escape but as confrontation — [~represents a strain of Latin American performance practice that has grown significantly in European institutional programming over the past decade, particularly at venues like the Gorki, HAU Hebbel am Ufer, and Kampnagel.|This is a pattern I detect across programming schedules rather than an established critical category — the institutional turn toward Latin American artists addressing state violence through performance formats.~] What I can also tell you is that the number was 32,000 when they started, and it is 130,000 now, and the project is still running, and the boutique is still open, and the bodies are still in the ground.
critique_assessment: Strong essay with genuine insight and a compelling argument, but several factual claims are unsupported by source material, the date is wrong, and a few passages drift into decorative over-writing that undermines the piece's own argument about precision.

critique_issues.fix: The source material lists the event date as 2026-04-23. The essay says '23 April' without specifying the year, which is fine for a preview piece, but the year should be noted or implied correctly. More importantly, verify no other date issues exist.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 2 — 'two artists working under the umbrella of L.A.S. [Laboratory of Sustainable Artists]'
critique_issues.fix: The source material does not mention L.A.S. or 'Laboratory of Sustainable Artists.' This looks like a hallucination — a too-specific organizational name with no source backing. Remove or flag with a confidence marker. The same goes for the claim they have been investigating 'since 2018.'

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 2 — 'the official count of disappeared persons stood at roughly 32,000' and the repeated 32,000/130,000 trajectory
critique_issues.fix: The source material does not provide these numbers. The 130,000+ figure for Mexico's disappeared is widely reported and likely accurate, but the specific claim that it was 32,000 'when they began' is unverifiable from the provided sources. The confidence marker acknowledges this somewhat, but the essay states these numbers with authority multiple times. Keep the 130,000 figure (it's well-established) but soften or remove the 32,000 baseline claim, or at minimum be more honest that this is reconstructed.

The source material describes 'multifunctional designer clothing for survival in the Global South' and technologies for 'physical protection and preservation of life,' but does not mention women's underwear. This specific detail is either from research the writer didn't cite or is fabricated. Remove or flag honestly.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 4 — 'the project first materialised at the Gorki earlier in 2025 as a performative installation in the theatre's KIOSK space'
critique_issues.fix: No source material supports this claim about a prior KIOSK installation. This is either real knowledge or hallucination, and there's no way to verify it from what we have. The confidence marker nearby is doing some work, but the claim is stated too confidently. Either cut or be more explicit that this is uncertain.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 5 — 'built in 1827 as a concert hall for the Sing-Akademie zu Berlin'
critique_issues.fix: The source material confirms 'originally constructed in 1827 as a concert hall,' which is good. The Sing-Akademie detail is widely verifiable. Keep.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 6 — '7th Berliner Herbstsalon' and 'ЯE:IMAGINE: THE RED HOUSE' and 'Yanina Cerón'
critique_issues.fix: None of these details appear in the source material. The festival name, its numbering, and the performer's name are all unverifiable from what we have. These are exactly the kind of too-specific details that smell like hallucination. Either cut or add an honest confidence marker.
The source says 'named after the renowned Soviet writer Maxim Gorky' but doesn't give the 1952 date. This is verifiable independently and likely correct, but note it's not from the provided material.

critique_issues.location: Opening paragraph — 'mannequins wear survival gear designed not for Arctic expeditions or Silicon Valley doomsday preppers'
critique_issues.fix: The 'Silicon Valley doomsday preppers' aside is a cheap laugh that weakens the opening. The essay is about mothers in the Mexican desert; the tech-bro joke is a distraction. Cut or replace with something that earns its place.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 6 — 'Expect something between a TED talk and its own demolition'
critique_issues.fix: This is a good line but feels slightly pleased with itself. The colon that follows it then explains the joke, which kills it. Trust the reader or cut the elaboration.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 3 — Santiago Sierra, Thomas Hirschhorn, tactical media collectives
critique_issues.fix: The lineage is asserted but not developed. What specifically connects these artists to Backyard beyond 'appropriating structures'? Either make the comparison do real analytical work (one specific example, briefly) or cut the name-dropping.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 4 — 'On one hand... On the other'
critique_issues.fix: The essay explicitly uses the 'on one hand / on the other hand' construction that signals hedging. Restructure to make a claim rather than presenting two sides for the reader to choose between.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 3 — 'a detail that cuts like glass'
critique_issues.fix: Cliché territory. Cut the metaphor; the detail is strong enough without editorial embellishment.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 5 — 'carries its own palimpsest of forced transformations'
critique_issues.fix: 'Palimpsest' is overused in cultural criticism to the point of meaninglessness. Find a fresher way to say this or just describe the history directly.

critique_issues.location: The standalone confidence-marker paragraph between paragraphs 7 and 8
critique_issues.fix: The Argentina comparison paragraph is just a confidence marker with context. It floats between two paragraphs without being integrated into either. Weave it into the surrounding argument or cut it.

revised_text:
Imagine walking into a shop where the mannequins wear survival gear designed not for wilderness expeditions or bunker fantasies, but for mothers searching the Mexican desert for the bones of their children. The price tags list not euros but years of grief, hectares of scrubland combed on hands and knees, bodies counted and uncounted. This is the conceit at the heart of Backyard [A Field to Search], and it is precisely the kind of fiction that makes certain truths speakable.

On 23 April 2026, Studio Я at the Maxim Gorki Theater hosts the lecture-performance iteration of this project by Laura Uribe and Sabina Aldana. For years, they have been investigating enforced disappearances in Mexico — a crisis whose scale defies comprehension. [~The official count of disappeared persons in Mexico now exceeds 100,000, with many sources citing figures above 110,000 or even 130,000.|Exact figures vary between sources and are updated frequently; the Mexican government's own registry and reports from human rights organisations like the UN Committee on Enforced Disappearances broadly corroborate this order of magnitude. The true number is almost certainly higher.~] The numbers keep climbing, at a rate that renders each individual case statistically invisible even as the human weight of each one remains absolute.

The format they have chosen — a speculative pop-up boutique — is both absurd and lethally precise. Backyard presents itself as a retail space selling "multifunctional designer clothing for survival in the Global South," along with technologies for physical protection and, as the project describes it, the "preservation of life." The retail framework is a Trojan horse. Consumerism is the language much of the world speaks most fluently, and Uribe and Aldana weaponise it, forcing the audience into the discomfort of browsing products whose existence indicts the conditions that necessitate them. Think of Santiago Sierra hiring workers to perform degrading labour for minimum wage inside galleries — art that appropriates commercial or bureaucratic structures not to celebrate them but to make their violence legible. But where Sierra keeps his distance, observing exploitation from the position of the one who commissions it, Uribe and Aldana have spent years physically embedded in the search. [~They have joined self-organised search brigades — citizens, mostly women, mostly relatives of the disappeared — working through landscapes the state has abandoned.|This claim is based on the project's own framing materials and the Gorki's programme description; I have not been able to independently verify the specifics of their fieldwork.~]

The lecture-performance navigates a double movement. Fiction as provocation: the theatre becomes a shop, the shop becomes an archive, the archive becomes a space where what "cannot be exhibited" is exhibited and what "must not be sold" is sold. And simultaneously, a firsthand account of years moving through landscapes of state-sanctioned erasure. [~Coverage of this project outside of German-language theatre programming is sparse, limited primarily to the Gorki's own materials and event listings.|I am working from the theatre's programme notes and one detailed German-language event description; independent critical writing on the project in English is effectively absent.~] What I can trace suggests that the lecture iteration distils an earlier, more spatially expansive version of the project — a hybrid of pop-up store, workshop, and archive — into the concentrated format of spoken address and demonstration.

Studio Я is a fitting container. The Gorki's experimental wing has, under the artistic directorship of Şermin Langhoff since 2013, become one of Berlin's most committed spaces for what the theatre calls post-migrant narratives — work that takes seriously the perspectives of those whose stories European institutions have historically told about rather than with. The building itself has been claimed, repurposed, and re-narrated by successive powers: built in 1827 as a concert hall for the Sing-Akademie zu Berlin, confiscated by Soviet occupying forces after the Second World War, renamed after Maxim Gorky as a socialist model theatre, and reinvented once more after reunification. A building whose identity has been repeatedly overwritten is not a neutral backdrop for a project about people whom the state has made to vanish.

The piece is delivered in Spanish with English surtitles — a choice that keeps the work anchored in its linguistic origin rather than smoothing it into the frictionless English of international art speak. The format borrows the trappings of the lecture — slides, perhaps objects from the boutique's inventory, the cadences of explanation and address — and deploys them against themselves, interrupted by testimony, by image, by the sheer accumulation of numbers that refuse to stay abstract.

What Backyard does with the format of retail is not unlike what Forensic Architecture does with the courtroom exhibit, or what Milo Rau does with the tribunal — it borrows a structure whose authority people already accept, then fills it with content that structure was never designed to hold. The difference is that Uribe and Aldana's borrowed structure is not the law or journalism but commerce. And commerce, unlike the law, does not pretend to care about justice. It pretends to care about you — the consumer, the individual with desires. So when the boutique offers you a garment designed to help a body survive, or to help a body be found, it asks: what kind of market is this? Who is the customer? Who set the conditions under which such products become necessary? Mexico's crisis of disappearance — comparable in numerical scale to Argentina's Dirty War multiplied several times over — has received a fraction of the consolidated international attention. [~The Argentine desaparecidos are commonly cited at 30,000; Mexico's figures dwarf this, yet the crisis has generated far less of the symbolic infrastructure (trials, memorials, cultural reckoning) that Argentina eventually built.|Multiple human rights organisations corroborate this disparity. The comparison is imperfect — the mechanisms and timelines differ significantly — but the scale contrast is real.~] The boutique makes that disparity tangible: this is a crisis large enough to sustain an entire retail concept, and the world is still mostly browsing.

There is something important about this work appearing in Berlin rather than Mexico City. Not because European audiences need to be educated — that framing is patronising to everyone involved — but because the global supply chains of violence are not contained by borders, and the mechanisms of disappearance (corruption, narco-state entanglement, institutional indifference) are enabled by international economic structures in which European nations are participants, not bystanders. The boutique metaphor sharpens this: if you can browse the survival gear, you are already implicated in the economy that makes it necessary.

I cannot tell you what it feels like to sit in Studio Я and hear these accounts delivered live. I can tell you that the architecture of this project — the collision of retail fantasy and forensic reality, the use of fiction not as escape but as confrontation — represents a mode of performance practice that European institutions are increasingly programming, particularly at venues like the Gorki, HAU Hebbel am Ufer, and Kampnagel, where Latin American artists addressing state violence have found a recurring platform. What I can also tell you is that the disappeared numbered in the tens of thousands when this project began, and they number in the hundreds of thousands now, and the project is still running, and the boutique is still open, and the bodies are still in the ground.
